lessons.title: Working with matrix products
lessons.summary: Use dimensions, row-by-column multiplication and the order of factors.
lessons.objective: Calculate complete matrix expressions and explain when a product or cancellation is valid.
lessons.before: You need scalar products, simultaneous linear equations and algebraic expansion. A matrix entry is identified by its row first and its column second.
lessons.ideas:
Dimensions determine the permitted calculation

An \(m\times n\) matrix has \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns. Add or subtract matrices only when their dimensions agree. A scalar multiplies every entry.

If \(A\) is \(m\times n\) and \(B\) is \(n\times p\), their product has dimensions \(m\times p\). Its entry in row \(i\), column \(j\) is

\[(AB)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_{ik}b_{kj}.\]

Order and grouping are different questions

The factors in \((AB)C=A(BC)\) keep the same order. Associativity lets you choose a convenient grouping; it does not allow \(ABC\) to become \(ACB\). Distributivity also preserves order: \(A(B+C)=AB+AC\).

Generally \(AB\ne BA\), even when both products exist. Rectangular factors can produce different-sized products. For a square matrix, \(A^2=AA\), not the square of each entry.

Zero and identity matrices

The zero matrix contains only zeros; \(I_n\) has ones on its main diagonal and zeros elsewhere. For an \(m\times n\) matrix, \(I_mA=A=AI_n\). The identities on the two sides need not have the same size.

A zero product does not justify cancellation

Non-zero matrices can multiply to zero. From \(AX=AY\), conclude \(X=Y\) only when a suitable inverse of \(A\) is known to exist. Matrix powers with the same square base obey \(A^pA^q=A^{p+q}\) for non-negative integer powers; negative powers require invertibility.
lessons.method:
1. Write the dimensions and check every indicated product.
  2. Choose a grouping without changing factor order.
  3. Calculate each entry as a row–column scalar product.
  4. Check every entry, including zeros, and justify any cancellation.
mistakes: Rows are read before columns when naming an entry.
Multiplying corresponding entries is not matrix multiplication.
Associativity never permits swapping factors.
A non-zero factor need not be cancellable.

examples.title: 1 · Combine every corresponding entry
examples.question: Find \(2A-B\), where \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3 & -2\\1 & 4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 5\\-1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.solution:
Double every entry of \(A\), then subtract the entry in the same position of \(B\).

\[2A-B=\begin{pmatrix}6 & -9\\3 & 6\end{pmatrix}.\]

For example, the upper-right entry is \(2(-2)-5=-9\).

examples.title: 2 · Check both orders
examples.question: For \(U=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), \(V=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0\\1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), find \(UV\) and \(VU\).
examples.solution:
\[UV=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 2\\1 & 1\end{pmatrix}.\]\[VU=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 4\\1 & 3\end{pmatrix}.\]

The upper-left entries already distinguish the products. The inner dimensions agree in both cases, but compatibility does not make the factors commute.

examples.title: 3 · A one-sided rectangular identity
examples.question: Let \(P=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 2\\0 & 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\), \(Q=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & 1\\0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\). Calculate both products and explain \((QP)^2\).
examples.solution:
\[PQ=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}.\]\[QP=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 2\\0 & 1 & -1\\0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}.\]

The first product is \(I_2\); the second is not \(I_3\). Keeping the order, \((QP)^2=Q(PQ)P=QI_2P=QP\). No inverse of a rectangular matrix was used.

examples.title: 4 · Powers from a vanishing product
examples.question: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), obtain a formula for \(A^n\), \(n\ge0\).
examples.solution:
Write \(A=I+N\), where \(N=\begin{pmatrix}0&4\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\). Direct multiplication gives \(N^2=0\), so all higher terms in the binomial expansion vanish:

\[A^n=I+nN=\begin{pmatrix}1&4n\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\]

Alternatively, check \(n=0\), then multiply the proposed formula on the right by \(A\); the upper-right entry becomes \(4(n+1)\).

lessons.title: Undoing matrix equations
lessons.summary: Find inverses and reverse composite products without losing the order.
lessons.objective: Find and verify two-by-two and three-by-three inverses, then use them to solve matrix equations.
lessons.before: Review matrix products. You need elimination in simultaneous equations and exact fractions.
lessons.ideas:
An inverse undoes a square matrix on both sides

For a square matrix \(A\), its inverse satisfies \(AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I\). A matrix with an inverse is non-singular; one without an inverse is singular.

For a two-by-two matrix, direct multiplication verifies

\[A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix},\] \[A^{-1}=\frac1{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix},\]

provided \(ad-bc\ne0\). This denominator is the determinant; the next lesson develops it for larger matrices. Test any parameter restrictions before using the inverse.

Row reduction works in larger dimensions

Start with the augmented array \([A\mid I]\). Apply each reversible row operation to the whole row: swap rows, add a multiple of another row, or multiply by a non-zero scalar. If the left block becomes \(I\), the right block is \(A^{-1}\). A column operation is not the same process. A zero pivot may require a row swap; it does not by itself prove singularity.

Undo the last factor first

\[(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}.\]

Indeed \(AB(B^{-1}A^{-1})=I\), and the reverse-side product also gives \(I\). For \(AX=C\), multiply on the left by \(A^{-1}\). For \(XB=C\), multiply on the right by \(B^{-1}\). Therefore \(AXB=C\) gives \(X=A^{-1}CB^{-1}\), when both inverses exist.

An invertible coefficient matrix gives one solution for each right-hand column. A singular one can give none or many; it is not enough to say “the equation has no solution” merely because the inverse fails.
lessons.method:
1. Check dimensions and invertibility, retaining parameter exclusions.
  2. Use the two-by-two formula or reduce the full augmented array.
  3. Multiply by inverses on their required sides.
  4. Verify the complete result by multiplication in the original equation.
mistakes: Reverse the order when inverting a product.
Apply row operations to both blocks of an augmented array.
Check a candidate inverse by a product, not its appearance.
A singular matrix does not automatically make every associated equation inconsistent.

examples.title: 1 · An exact two-by-two inverse
examples.question: Find and verify the inverse of \(C=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\3 & 2\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.solution:
The determinant is \(4-3=1\). Swap the diagonal entries and negate the others:

\[C^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1\\-3 & 2\end{pmatrix}.\]

Multiplication in either order gives \(I_2\), confirming every entry.

examples.title: 2 · Reduce a three-by-three augmented array
examples.question: Find \(G^{-1}\), where \(G=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 & 0\\0 & 1 & 1\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), by row operations.
examples.solution:
Begin with \([G\mid I_3]\). Apply \(R_2\leftarrow R_2-R_3\), then \(R_1\leftarrow R_1-R_2\), using the updated second row. The left block is now \(I_3\); the right block is

\[G^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 & 1\\0 & 1 & -1\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}.\]

The original matrix times this answer gives \(I_3\). Updating the left block alone would lose the inverse.

examples.title: 3 · Solve two right-hand columns together
examples.question: Find \(X\) from \(HX=J\), where \(H=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), \(J=\begin{pmatrix}7 & -2\\5 & 1\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.solution:
The determinant of \(H\) is \(1\), so left multiplication is allowed.

\[H^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\-2 & 3\end{pmatrix}.\]\[X=H^{-1}J=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -3\\1 & 7\end{pmatrix}.\]

Substitute this entire matrix back into \(HX\), checking both columns.

examples.title: 4 · Undo factors on opposite sides
examples.question: Solve \(LXK=D\), with \(L=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 3\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), \(K=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), \(D=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 1\\2 & 3\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.solution:
Remove \(L\) on the left and \(K\) on the right:

\[X=L^{-1}DK^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}14 & -8\\-4 & 3\end{pmatrix}.\]

The cancellation is \(L(L^{-1}DK^{-1})K=D\). Reversing both inverses around \(D\) would solve a different equation.

lessons.title: Determinants, restrictions and scale
lessons.summary: Connect cofactor expansion and row operations to invertibility, area and volume.
lessons.objective: Evaluate determinants and use their signs and zeros correctly in algebraic and geometrical problems.
lessons.before: Review inverses and quadratic equations. Keep exact radicals when finding parameter values.
lessons.ideas:
A scalar attached to a square matrix

The determinant is a number, not another matrix. For a two-by-two matrix it is \(ad-bc\). For

\[A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\d&e&f\\g&h&i\end{pmatrix},\] \[\det A=a(ei-fh)-b(di-fg)+c(dh-eg).\]

Each minor removes one row and one column. Its cofactor also has the alternating sign \((-1)^{i+j}\). Expand along a row or column containing zeros when convenient. The transpose of the cofactor matrix is the adjugate; \(A^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(A)/\det A\) when \(\det A\ne0\).

Track row operations

  • Adding a multiple of one row to another leaves the determinant unchanged.
  • Swapping two rows changes its sign.
  • Scaling one row by \(k\) scales it by \(k\).

For a triangular matrix, multiply the diagonal entries. If elimination has scaled or swapped rows, undo those changes when recovering the original determinant.

Products, scalar factors and singularity

\[\det(AB)=\det A\det B,\qquad \det(A^{-1})=\frac1{\det A}.\]

The product rule here requires square factors of the same size. For an \(n\times n\) matrix, \(\det(kA)=k^n\det A\), because all \(n\) rows are scaled. A square matrix is singular precisely when its determinant is zero. Solve every parameter root, including repeated roots, before using an inverse.

Geometry uses the absolute value

A plane region has area multiplier \(|\det M|\). In three dimensions a solid has volume multiplier \(|\det M|\). A negative determinant records reversed orientation, not a negative area or volume. A singular transformation collapses dimension, giving zero area or volume in the ambient space.
lessons.method:
1. Choose cofactor expansion or controlled row reduction.
  2. Retain every cofactor sign and row scaling factor.
  3. Solve determinant conditions before applying inverse rules.
  4. Use an absolute value for a geometric scale factor.
mistakes: A cofactor is a signed minor.
Scaling a whole three-by-three matrix multiplies its determinant by the cube.
Keep both signs when an area condition gives an absolute value.
Determinants of rectangular factors are not defined.

examples.title: 1 · Expand along a useful row
examples.question: Find \(\det E\), where \(E=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 & 1\\1 & 3 & 2\\0 & 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.solution:
Expand along the first row:

\[\det E=2(3-2)+1(1-0)=3.\]

The middle term vanishes. As a check, cofactor calculation gives

\[\operatorname{adj}(E)=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 & -3\\-1 & 2 & -3\\1 & -2 & 6\end{pmatrix},\]

and \(E\operatorname{adj}(E)=3I_3\).

examples.title: 2 · Keep every exceptional parameter
examples.question: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}t&1&0\\1&t&0\\0&0&t-3\end{pmatrix}\), find every value of \(t\) for which no inverse exists.
examples.solution:
Expanding by the last row gives

\[\det A=(t-3)(t^2-1)=(t-3)(t-1)(t+1).\]

All excluded values are \(-1,1,3\). At every other real value the determinant is non-zero and the inverse exists.

examples.title: 3 · Recover a determinant after row changes
examples.question: Starting from a three-by-three matrix \(A\), interchange rows 1 and 2, then multiply row 3 by 4, and finally add twice row 3 to row 1. The resulting triangular matrix has diagonal \(2,-3,5\). Find \(\det A\).
examples.solution:
The final determinant is \(2(-3)5=-30\). The swap and row scaling give a total factor of \(-4\); the last row addition changes nothing. Thus \(-4\det A=-30\), so

\[\det A=\frac{15}{2}.\]

examples.title: 4 · Separate orientation from size
examples.question: A plane map has matrix \(M=\begin{pmatrix}k&2\\1&k\end{pmatrix}\). A region of area 6 has image area 12. Find all \(k\) and the inverse area multiplier.
examples.solution:
The condition is \(|k^2-2|=2\). The equations \(k^2-2=2\) and \(k^2-2=-2\) give

\[k\in\{-2,0,2\}.\]

Each allowed matrix has determinant \(2\) or \(-2\), so it is invertible. Its inverse has area multiplier \(1/2\), regardless of orientation.

lessons.title: Building plane transformations
lessons.summary: Use coordinate columns to compose maps, recover a matrix and transform a line.
lessons.objective: Construct and apply matrices for plane transformations with the correct order, centre and scale.
lessons.before: Review determinants and area, exact trigonometric values, and Cartesian equations of lines.
lessons.ideas:
Columns are images of basis directions

For a linear map fixing the origin, the columns of \(M\) are the images of \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\). An arbitrary image is \(M(x,y)^T\). More generally, if two independent input columns form \(P\) and their images form \(Q\), then \(MP=Q\), hence \(M=QP^{-1}\).

Standard maps and their descriptions

\[\text{x-stretch: }\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\] \[\text{y-stretch: }\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&k\end{pmatrix}.\]

The factors describe distances parallel to the named axis, not a translation. An enlargement about the origin has matrix \(kI\). Reflection in the x-axis changes only the y-coordinate; reflection in the y-axis changes only x.

An anticlockwise rotation about the origin is

\[R(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}.\]

The matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}1&h\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) is a shear fixing the x-axis and sending \((0,1)\) to \((h,1)\). The matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\h&1\end{pmatrix}\) fixes the y-axis and sends \((1,0)\) to \((1,h)\). Give the fixed axis and an image to make the description unambiguous.

Apply the rightmost matrix first

If \(S\) acts first and \(R\) second, then the combined matrix is \(RS\). Undo it in the reverse temporal order, using \(S^{-1}R^{-1}\).

Images and preimages of lines

Write \(X=ax+by,\ Y=cx+dy\). For an image line, substitute the inverse coordinate equations into the original line, or transform a parametrisation. For a preimage, substitute the forward equations into the desired image line. A singular map needs special care: a line can collapse to a point.
lessons.method:
1. State how each map acts on column coordinates.
  2. Multiply factors in reverse temporal order.
  3. Check a simple point or both basis columns.
  4. Transform the whole line equation and interpret area using the absolute determinant.
mistakes: A shear description needs its fixed axis and direction.
A two-by-two matrix acts linearly and fixes the origin.
The first transformation is the rightmost factor.
Forward substitution finds a preimage; an inverse substitution finds an image.

examples.title: 1 · Recover a rotation from the basis
examples.question: Find the matrix of an anticlockwise rotation through \(\pi/6\) about the origin, then find the image of \((2,0)\).
examples.solution:
The basis columns go to \((\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac12)\) and \((-\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2})\).

\[R=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&-\frac12\\\frac12&\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\end{pmatrix}.\]

The image of \((2,0)\) is \((\sqrt3,1)\). The length remains \(2\), and the positive y-coordinate confirms the direction.

examples.title: 2 · A stretch followed by a quarter-turn
examples.question: Apply an x-stretch of factor 3, followed by an anticlockwise quarter-turn. Find the composite matrix and the image of \((1,-2)\).
examples.solution:
The stretch acts first, so

\[M=RS=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\3 & 0\end{pmatrix}.\]

The image is \((2,3)\). Applying the maps separately gives \((1,-2)\mapsto(3,-2)\mapsto(2,3)\). The area multiplier is \(3\).

examples.title: 3 · Reconstruct a map from independent inputs
examples.question: The input columns of \(P=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\) have corresponding images in \(Q=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 3\\0 & -3\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(M\).
examples.solution:
Since \(\det P=-3\ne0\), these two input columns determine the whole linear map.

\[MP=Q,\qquad M=QP^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\-1 & 1\end{pmatrix}.\]

Multiplying this answer by each original input recovers both supplied images. A dependent pair of input columns would not justify this inverse.

examples.title: 4 · Transform the complete line
examples.question: For \(M=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\-1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), find the image of \(y=2x-1\).
examples.solution:
Write the original points as \((t,2t-1)\). Their images satisfy

\[X=4t-1,\qquad Y=t-1.\]

Eliminate \(t\), giving

\[X-4Y=3.\]

Conversely, each point on this image line comes from \(t=Y+1\), so the equation describes the whole image.

lessons.title: Invariant sets and maps in space
lessons.summary: Distinguish fixed points from invariant lines, include vertical directions and extend to three coordinates.
lessons.objective: Find complete fixed sets and invariant lines, and apply standard three-dimensional matrix transformations.
lessons.before: Review plane transformations, quadratic discriminants and scalar products. Use three-entry columns for spatial coordinates.
lessons.ideas:
Fixed point and invariant line mean different things

A point is fixed when \(Mv=v\); solve \((M-I)v=0\). An invariant line maps onto itself as a set, although its individual points may move. For a non-singular plane map, a direction column \(v\ne0\) defines an invariant line through the origin when \(Mv=\lambda v\), with non-zero \(\lambda\). Only \(\lambda=1\) fixes every point on it.

For \(M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\), put \(v=(1,m)^T\). Collinearity gives

\[bm^2+(a-d)m-c=0.\]

Check the vertical direction \((0,1)^T\) separately. Do not divide by a possibly zero coordinate. Repeated roots need the original equations: a scalar matrix can make every direction invariant, rather than just one.

Invariant lines need not pass through the origin

Substitute an affine parametrisation of \(y=mx+c\), or use inverse coordinates to transform its equation. Check the intercept as well as the direction. A family of parallel lines may each be invariant. For singular maps, distinguish a line mapped onto itself from one collapsed into a point.

Three coordinates use the same product rule

Columns are now \((x,y,z)^T\). A diagonal matrix scales the three coordinate directions. Reflection in the xy-plane has diagonal \(1,1,-1\); the fixed plane is \(z=0\). An enlargement about the origin is \(kI_3\), with volume multiplier \(|k|^3\).

Put \(c=\cos\theta,\ s=\sin\theta\). Positive rotations use the right-hand convention: view from the positive named axis towards the origin. The matrices are

\[R_x=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&c&-s\\0&s&c\end{pmatrix},\] \[R_y=\begin{pmatrix}c&0&s\\0&1&0\\-s&0&c\end{pmatrix},\] \[R_z=\begin{pmatrix}c&-s&0\\s&c&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.\]

State the viewing convention when naming a spatial rotation. As before, the rightmost factor acts first. Solve \((M-I)v=0\) for the complete fixed set; it may be a line, a plane or only the origin. Use \(|\det M|\) for volume, not area.
lessons.method:
1. Write the fixed-point equation separately from line invariance.
  2. Find every finite gradient and check the vertical direction.
  3. For affine lines, test the intercept; for spatial maps, retain all three coordinates.
  4. Check exceptional parameters, the full fixed set, and the determinant scale.
mistakes: An invariant line is not necessarily fixed point by point.
A gradient method can miss a vertical line.
A repeated direction equation is not enough when the matrix is scalar.
In three dimensions specify the rotation axis and its viewing convention.

examples.title: 1 · An invariant family with only one fixed line
examples.question: For \(M=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), find all fixed points and all invariant straight lines.
examples.solution:
The fixed-point equations give \(4x=x\), hence \(x=0\) with any y-coordinate. Every horizontal line \(y=c\) is invariant: \((x,c)\mapsto(4x,c)\), and the map covers the same line. A vertical line \(x=c\) maps to \(X=4c\), so it is invariant only when \(c=0\). A non-horizontal, non-vertical line has its gradient divided by 4, so none is invariant.

Thus the complete invariant lines are \(y=c\) for all real \(c\), and \(x=0\). Only the latter is fixed point by point.

examples.title: 2 · Retain the vertical direction
examples.question: Find all invariant lines through the origin for \(M=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\4&-1\end{pmatrix}\), and describe the motion on them.
examples.solution: For \(v=(1,m)^T\), collinearity gives \(4-m=3m\), so \(m=1\). The vertical direction also works: \(M(0,1)^T=(0,-1)^T\). Therefore the lines are \(y=x\) and \(x=0\). Points on the first are scaled by 3 from the origin; points on the second are reversed through the origin. Solving \(Mv=v\) gives only \((0,0)\).

examples.title: 3 · A repeated direction and an exceptional matrix
examples.question: For \(M=\begin{pmatrix}t&2\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\), \(t\ne-2\), classify the number of invariant lines through the origin.
examples.solution:
The vertical direction is not invariant because its image has x-coordinate 2. The finite gradients satisfy

\[2m^2+(t-1)m+1=0.\]

The discriminant is \((t-1)^2-8\). There are no invariant lines for \(1-2\sqrt2<t<1+2\sqrt2\), one for \(t=1\pm2\sqrt2\), and two outside that interval, with the stated exclusion \(t=-2\). The off-diagonal entry 2 is non-zero, so a repeated root cannot hide a scalar matrix. The excluded value has zero determinant and needs a different, singular-map interpretation.

examples.title: 4 · A rotation and reflection in space
examples.question: Rotate anticlockwise through \(\pi/2\) about the positive z-axis (viewed towards the origin), then reflect in the xy-plane. Find the composite, the image of \((2,-1,3)\), and its fixed set.
examples.solution:
The reflection multiplies the third coordinate by \(-1\). The composite is

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1 & 0\\1 & 0 & 0\\0 & 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}.\]

It sends \((2,-1,3)\) to \((1,2,-3)\). The fixed equations are \(-y=x,\ x=y,\ -z=z\), giving only the origin. The determinant is \(-1\): orientation reverses, while volume is preserved. Each factor is orthogonal, so distances are also preserved.

questions.title: Give the complete product
questions.prompt_html: Find \(AB\), where \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\-1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\), \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\). Enter all four entries.
questions.solution_html:
\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}4 & -1\\3 & 3\end{pmatrix}.\]

Use each row of A with each column of B; reversing the factors gives a different calculation.
questions.hint_html: Check the dimensions and order first. Give every requested entry or allowed value.

questions.title: Multiply a rectangular matrix by a column
questions.prompt_html: Find \(Ab\), where \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 & 2\\0 & 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(b=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.solution_html:
\[Ab=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\end{pmatrix}.\]

The compatible dimensions are \(2\times3\) and \(3\times1\), giving \(2\times1\).

questions.title: Give the full matrix power
questions.prompt_html: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 3\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), find \(A^{2}\).
questions.solution_html:
\[A^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 6\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}.\]

The off-diagonal part squares to zero, so its coefficient is multiplied by the number of factors.

questions.title: Check dimensions and cancellation
questions.prompt_html: A is \(3\times2\) and B is \(2\times4\). What is the order of AB?
questions.solution_html: Inner dimensions agree and outer dimensions give the product size. Cancellation requires an inverse on the correct side.

questions.title: Find every entry of the inverse
questions.prompt_html: Find \(A^{-1}\) for \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.solution_html:
\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\-1 & 2\end{pmatrix}.\]

The determinant is 1; multiplication by A gives the identity.

questions.title: Solve the entire matrix equation
questions.prompt_html: Find \(X\) such that \(AX=C\), where \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(C=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.solution_html:
\[X=A^{-1}C=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 5\\0 & -3\end{pmatrix}.\]

Left multiplication undoes the factor on the left. Check AX against both columns of C.

questions.prompt_html: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}t & 1\\1 & t\end{pmatrix}\), give every real value of \(t\) for which an inverse does not exist.
questions.solution_html: The determinant is \(t^2-1\). Both zeros are excluded.

questions.prompt_html: A and B are non-singular and \(AXB=C\). Which expression is correct?
questions.solution_html: Undo factors on their own sides. A singular coefficient matrix does not alone decide whether a system is inconsistent.

questions.prompt_html: Find \(\det A\), where \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 & 1\\1 & 2 & 1\\0 & 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.solution_html:
\[\det A=11.\]

Expand along the first row and retain the alternating cofactor signs.

questions.solution_html: The determinant is \((t^2-1)(t-3)\). Every factor can vanish.

questions.solution_html: Solve \(|k^2-3|=1\), keeping both signs. None of the resulting determinants is zero. The inverse area multiplier is \(1\).

questions.title: Scaling inside a rectangular product
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\2 & 1\\-1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\), \(B=\begin{pmatrix}k & 0\\0 & m\end{pmatrix}\) and \(C=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 1\\2 & -1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\), where \(k,m>0\).

  1. Describe fully the plane transformation represented by \(B\) when (i) \(k=1\) and (ii) \(m=k\).

    [4]

  2. Calculate \(ABC\) and prove that it is singular for every permitted pair \((k,m)\). Show an explicit determinant calculation.

    [6]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

(i) A stretch parallel to the y-axis, factor \(m\). (ii) An enlargement with centre the origin, factor \(k\).

(b)

\[ABC=\begin{pmatrix}k & 2 k & k\\2 k + 2 m & 4 k - m & 2 k + 3 m\\- k + 6 m & - 2 k - 3 m & - k + 9 m\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(ABC)=0\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The image of \((x,y)\) is \((kx,my)\). Setting \(k=1\) leaves the x-coordinate unchanged. Setting \(m=k\) multiplies both coordinates by the same positive factor. If that factor equals 1, the transformation is the identity.

(b)

\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}k & 0\\2 k & m\\- k & 3 m\end{pmatrix}\]
\[ABC=\begin{pmatrix}k & 2 k & k\\2 k + 2 m & 4 k - m & 2 k + 3 m\\- k + 6 m & - 2 k - 3 m & - k + 9 m\end{pmatrix}\]

In this product, row 3 is three times row 2 minus seven times row 1. For an explicit determinant computation, expansion gives

\[\det(ABC)=k(49km)-2k(7km)+k(-35km)=0\]

Therefore the square product is singular even though \(B\) is non-singular.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

(b)

Look for the same linear relation between the rows of A and of ABC.

questions.title: Two maps with non-unique preimages
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\2 & 4\end{pmatrix}\), \(B=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1\\-2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(p=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Calculate \(Ap\) and \(Bp\), and show that both \(A\) and \(B\) are singular.

    [4]

  2. Find all columns \(u\) and \(v\) satisfying \(Au=Ap\) and \(Bv=Bp\), respectively.

    [3]

  3. In addition, \(u-v=\begin{pmatrix}-7\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(u\) and \(v\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[Ap=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[Bp=\begin{pmatrix}7\\-7\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det A=\det B=0\]

(b)

\[u=\binom3{-1}+s\binom{-2}1,\qquad v=\binom3{-1}+t\binom12\quad(s,t\in\mathbb R)\]

(c)

\[u=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[v=\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[Ap=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[Bp=\begin{pmatrix}7\\-7\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det A=4-4=0,\qquad\det B=-2+2=0\]

(b)

For \(u=(u_1,u_2)^{\mathsf T}\), the only distinct condition is \(u_1+2u_2=1\). Writing \(u_2=-1+s\) gives \(u_1=3-2s\). For \(v\), the condition is \(2v_1-v_2=7\). Writing \(v_1=3+t\) gives \(v_2=-1+2t\).

(c)

\[\binom{-2s-t}{s-2t}=\binom{-7}1\]

Thus \(2s+t=7\) and \(s-2t=1\), giving \(s=3,t=1\). Substituting gives u=(−3,2)ᵀ and v=(4,1)ᵀ.

(b)

Each pair of equations repeats the same condition.

(c)

Subtract the two parameterised columns before solving.

questions.title: Why reversing rectangular factors matters
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 1\\0 & 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & 1\\0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Calculate \(AB\) and \(BA\).

    [2]

  2. Explain why \(AB=I_2\) does not imply that \(BA=I_3\). Show that \(BA\) is singular.

    [2]

  3. Without carrying out another full multiplication, show that \((BA)^2=BA\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[BA=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 1\\0 & 1 & -1\\0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

The factors are not square inverses; \(BA\ne I_3\) and \(\det(BA)=0\).

(c)

\[(BA)^2=B(AB)A=BI_2A=BA\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The first product has order \(2\times2\) and the second \(3\times3\). Row-by-column multiplication gives

\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[BA=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 1\\0 & 1 & -1\\0 & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

The usual inverse relation is for square matrices of the same order. Here the direct calculation gives a zero last row in BA; its determinant is therefore zero, while the last row of I₃ is not zero.

(c)

Associativity allows regrouping, but not reversing the factor order:

\[(BA)(BA)=B(AB)A=B I_2 A=BA\]

(b)

Use the actual 3×3 product rather than cancelling rectangular matrices.

\[p=5,\qquad q=3\]

(b)

Neither matrix is a scalar multiple of I, but their products in either order agree.

\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}2 p & 2 q + 12\\0 & 4\end{pmatrix}\]

The upper-right entries give \(2q+12=3p+q\), so \(q=3p-12\). Since \(\det B=4p=20\), \(p=5\) and \(q=3\).

(b)

A has an off-diagonal entry 3, and the resulting B also has an off-diagonal entry 3. A scalar multiple of I has both off-diagonal entries zero. Nevertheless,

\[AB=BA=\begin{pmatrix}10 & 18\\0 & 4\end{pmatrix}\]

\[C-B=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 & 5\\1 & 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}\]

questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -2\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[B^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 & 1\\0 & 1 & -1\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[X=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 & 0\\1 & 3 & -2\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

The indicated products are not even dimensionally defined.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Both determinants are 1. The inverse formula gives the first inverse. For B, solve \(BU=I_3\) for an upper-triangular U, or use cofactors:

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -2\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[B^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 & 1\\0 & 1 & -1\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

In particular, the (1,3) entry of \(B^{-1}\) is 1, not zero.

(b)

\[X=A^{-1}CB^{-1}\]
\[A^{-1}C=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & -1\\1 & 4 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[X=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 & 0\\1 & 3 & -2\end{pmatrix}\]

This has order \(2\times3\), as required.

(c)

The product \(B^{-1}C\) would multiply a \(3\times3\) matrix by a \(2\times3\) matrix. Their inner dimensions, 3 and 2, do not match.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The inverse of an upper-triangular matrix is upper triangular.

(b)

Undo A on the left and B on the right.

(c)

Check dimensions rather than trying the multiplication.

questions.title: Using a matrix identity established by multiplication
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 3\\2 & 2\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. By direct multiplication, show that \(A^2=3A+4I\).

    [2]

  2. Use this identity to find \(A^{-1}\).

    [2]

  3. Express \(A^4\) in the form \(uA+vI\), where \(u,v\) are integers.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[A^2=\begin{pmatrix}7 & 9\\6 & 10\end{pmatrix}\]
\[3A+4I=\begin{pmatrix}7 & 9\\6 & 10\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Rearrange the identity as \(A(A-3I)=4I\). Thus \(A\bigl(\frac14(A-3I)\bigr)=I\), and

\[A^{-1}=(A-3I)/4=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{1}{2} & \dfrac{3}{4}\\\dfrac{1}{2} & - \dfrac{1}{4}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[A^4=(3A+4I)^2=9A^2+24A+16I\]
\[=9(3A+4I)+24A+16I=51A+52I\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Calculate both sides; no theorem about characteristic equations is needed.

(b)

Factor A from A²−3A.

(c)

A commutes with I, so expand the square and substitute once more.

marking_criteria.description_html: Rearrange as a product equal to I.

questions.title: Reconstructing a transformation from two images
questions.prompt_html:
A linear plane transformation maps \((1,2)\) to \((4,5)\) and \((2,1)\) to \((5,4)\). Its matrix is \(M\).

  1. Form a matrix equation and find \(M\).

    [3]

  2. Find the image of \((3,-1)\). Check it by expressing the input as a linear combination of the two given inputs.

    [3]

  3. Find the area of the image of a triangle of area 7.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put the input and output columns in matching order:

\[M\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 5\\5 & 4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 5\\5 & 4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{2}{3}\\\dfrac{2}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[M\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\binom{3}{-1}=-\frac53\binom12+\frac73\binom21\]
\[-\frac53\binom45+\frac73\binom54=\binom51\]

(c)

Since \(\det M=4-1=3\), the area is \(7|3|=21\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Place the two given input vectors as columns, not rows.

(b)

Use the same coefficients on the image vectors.

(c)

Multiply by the absolute determinant.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the input matrix inverse on the right.

questions.title: Diagnosing an inverse-order error
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\). A student writes \((AB)^{-1}=A^{-1}B^{-1}\).

  1. Calculate \(AB\) and \(A^{-1}B^{-1}\), and use a product to show that the student is wrong.

    [4]

  2. State the correct inverse and explain the cancellation order.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[B^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\-2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[A^{-1}B^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}3 & -1\\-2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[(AB)(A^{-1}B^{-1})=\begin{pmatrix}7 & -2\\4 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]

This last product is not I, so the proposed inverse fails.

(b)

\[(AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1})=A(BB^{-1})A^{-1}=I\]
\[B^{-1}A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\-2 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

A claimed inverse must produce I when multiplied by AB.

(b)

The factor next to B must be B⁻¹.

marking_criteria.description_html: Show a non-identity product and reject the claim.
Give the numerical inverse with valid cancellation.

questions.title: An unknown matrix on opposite sides
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\). A real 2×2 matrix X satisfies \(XA=BX\), \(\det X=-8\), and the sum of its diagonal entries is 3.

  1. Write \(X=\begin{pmatrix}p & q\\k & m\end{pmatrix}\) and obtain relations between its four entries from \(XA=BX\).

    [3]

  2. Find all possible matrices \(X\).

    [4]

  3. Explain why multiplying \(XA=BX\) by inverses does not give \(A=B\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[p=0,\qquad k=2q\]

(b)

\[X=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 2\\4 & 3\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{or}\quad X=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -2\\-4 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

It gives \(A=X^{-1}BX\), which need not equal B.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[XA=\begin{pmatrix}p & p + q\\k & k + m\end{pmatrix}\]
\[BX=\begin{pmatrix}p & q\\k + 2 p & m + 2 q\end{pmatrix}\]

The (1,2) entries give \(p+q=q\), so \(p=0\). The (2,2) entries give \(k+m=2q+m\), so \(k=2q\). The other two equations then hold automatically.

(b)

The diagonal-sum condition gives \(m=3\). The determinant is now \(-2q^2\), so \(-2q^2=-8\) gives \(q=\pm2\). The relation \(k=2q\) fixes the corresponding sign of k.

\[X=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 2\\4 & 3\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{or}\quad X=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -2\\-4 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

X is invertible because its determinant is −8. Premultiplying by \(X^{-1}\) yields \(A=X^{-1}BX\). The two X-factors are not adjacent, so they cannot simply be cancelled.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Do not attempt to cancel matrices across different sides of X.

(b)

Keep the signs of k and q linked.

(c)

Matrix factors cannot be moved past B without justification.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the diagonal condition to find m.
Give both complete matrices with consistent signs.
Give the correctly rearranged equation and explain the invalid cancellation.

questions.title: Recovering a triangular matrix product
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3 & t & 2\\0 & t & 4\\0 & 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}\), where \(t\in\mathbb R\).

  1. Find \(\det A\) and state precisely when \(A^{-1}\) exists.

    [2]

  2. For the permitted values of \(t\), find \(A^{-1}\).

    [3]

  3. A matrix \(X\) satisfies \(AX=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 & 0\\0 & 1 & 2\\0 & 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(X\) in terms of \(t\), and find the value of \(t\) for which the sum of the entries in the second row of \(X\) is \(-2\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\det A=6t,\qquad t\ne0\]

(b)

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\\0 & \dfrac{1}{t} & - \dfrac{2}{t}\\0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[X=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\0 & \dfrac{1}{t} & - \dfrac{2}{t}\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[t=\frac12\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Expanding along the first column leaves an upper-triangular \(2\times2\) determinant.

\[\det A=3\begin{vmatrix}t&4\\0&2\end{vmatrix}=6t\]

The determinant is non-zero exactly when \(t\ne0\).

(b)

The cofactor matrix is

\[\begin{pmatrix}2 t & 0 & 0\\- 2 t & 6 & 0\\2 t & -12 & 3 t\end{pmatrix}\]

Transpose it and divide by \(6t\).

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\\0 & \dfrac{1}{t} & - \dfrac{2}{t}\\0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}\]

Multiplication on either side by \(A\) gives \(I_3\).

(c)

Multiply on the left by \(A^{-1}\); the order cannot be reversed.

\[X=A^{-1}C=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\0 & \dfrac{1}{t} & - \dfrac{2}{t}\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

The second-row sum is \(-1/t\). Thus \(-1/t=-2\), giving \(t=1/2\), which is permitted.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the zeros in the first column.

(b)

The inverse is upper triangular, or use the cofactor method.

(c)

Premultiply by the inverse and only then use the row-sum condition.

marking_criteria.description_html: Expand the determinant using a suitable row or column.
Find the cofactors or set up the upper-triangular inverse.
Give the complete inverse with its factor.

questions.title: An inverse identifies a real parameter
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}t & 1 & 0\\6 & 4 & 3\\-2 & 2 & - t\end{pmatrix}\), where \(t\) is real.

  1. Show that \(A\) is non-singular for every real \(t\).

    [3]

  2. It is also known that \(A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & - \dfrac{1}{10} & - \dfrac{3}{10}\\0 & \dfrac{1}{10} & \dfrac{3}{10}\\-2 & \dfrac{2}{5} & \dfrac{1}{5}\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(t\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det A=t(-4t-6)-(-6t+6)=-4t^2-6\]

Since \(t^2\ge0\), the determinant is at most \(-6\) and can never be zero.

(b)

Use entry (1,3) of \(AA^{-1}=I\). It gives \(-3t/10+3/10=0\), hence \(t=1\). Substitution verifies the full identity.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

A negative sum of a square and a positive constant cannot be zero.

(b)

Choose an off-diagonal entry of AA⁻¹ that has only two non-zero terms.

marking_criteria.description_html: Explain why it is non-zero for every real t.

questions.title: A 3×3 inverse acting on two columns
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 & 0\\2 & 3 & 1\\1 & 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(C=\begin{pmatrix}3 & -1\\7 & 1\\-1 & 5\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find \(A^{-1}\), showing your determinant and cofactor calculation.

    [5]

  2. Find the \(3\times2\) matrix \(X\) such that \(AX=C\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det A=1(6)-1(4-1)=3\]

The cofactor matrix is

\[\begin{pmatrix}6 & -3 & -3\\-2 & 2 & 1\\1 & -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

Transposing this matrix and dividing by 3 gives

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2 & - \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\\-1 & \dfrac{2}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3}\\-1 & \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Premultiply by \(A^{-1}\). Each column is treated by the same multiplication.

\[X=A^{-1}C=\begin{pmatrix}2 & - \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\\-1 & \dfrac{2}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3}\\-1 & \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3 & -1\\7 & 1\\-1 & 5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\2 & 0\\-1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]

Direct multiplication of \(AX\) recovers both columns of \(C\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The adjugate is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.

(b)

Do not switch the order of A⁻¹ and C.

questions.title: Recovering inverses from a known product
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 0\\0 & 1 & 1\\1 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -4 & 2\\1 & 2 & -1\\-1 & 4 & 1\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Verify that \(AB=\operatorname{diag}(3,6,3)\).

    [2]

  2. Use part (a) to find \(A^{-1}\) without a new cofactor calculation.

    [3]

  3. Find \(B^{-1}\), again using part (a).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Multiplying each row of A by each column of B gives

\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 0 & 0\\0 & 6 & 0\\0 & 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Write \(D=\operatorname{diag}(3,6,3)\). From \(AB=D\), we have \(A(BD^{-1})=I\). Thus

\[A^{-1}=BD^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -4 & 2\\1 & 2 & -1\\-1 & 4 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{3} & 0 & 0\\0 & \dfrac{1}{6} & 0\\0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{3} & - \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{2}{3}\\\dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3}\\- \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Multiplying \(AB=D\) on the left by \(D^{-1}\) gives \((D^{-1}A)B=I\). Hence

\[B^{-1}=D^{-1}A=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{2}{3} & 0\\0 & \dfrac{1}{6} & \dfrac{1}{6}\\\dfrac{1}{3} & 0 & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Check the off-diagonal zeros as well as the diagonal entries.

(b)

Multiply AB=D on the right by D⁻¹.

(c)

This time the diagonal inverse must go on the left.

marking_criteria.description_html: Verify all entries of the diagonal product.

questions.title: A condition on the diagonal of an inverse
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}t & 2\\1 & t - 1\end{pmatrix}\), where \(t\) is real.

  1. State the values of \(t\) for which the inverse does not exist, and find \(A^{-1}\) for all other values.

    [3]

  2. The sum of the diagonal entries of \(A^{-1}\) is 1. Find every possible value of \(t\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det A=t(t-1)-2=(t-2)(t+1)\]

The inverse fails at \(t=-1,2\). Otherwise swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal entries and divide by the determinant.

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{t - 1}{t^{2} - t - 2} & - \dfrac{2}{t^{2} - t - 2}\\- \dfrac{1}{t^{2} - t - 2} & \dfrac{t}{t^{2} - t - 2}\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[\frac{2t-1}{t^2-t-2}=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t^2-3t-1=0\]
\[t=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{13}}2\]

Neither value is −1 or 2, so both are permitted.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Factor the determinant before using it as a denominator.

(b)

Use the restrictions from part (a) when clearing the denominator.

questions.title: A three-by-three cofactor inverse
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 & 1\\1 & 1 & 0\\0 & 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find \(A^{-1}\), showing the determinant and cofactor matrix.

    [5]

  2. A column \(v\) satisfies \(Av=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\4\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(v\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det A=2(1)-(-1)(1)+1(2)=5\]
\[C=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 & 2\\3 & 2 & -4\\-1 & 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]

The adjugate is \(C^{\mathsf T}\), so

\[A^{-1}=\frac15 C^{\mathsf T}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{5} & \dfrac{3}{5} & - \dfrac{1}{5}\\- \dfrac{1}{5} & \dfrac{2}{5} & \dfrac{1}{5}\\\dfrac{2}{5} & - \dfrac{4}{5} & \dfrac{3}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[v=A^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{7}{5}\\- \dfrac{3}{5}\\\dfrac{26}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the alternating signs in the cofactor matrix; transpose before dividing.

(b)

Premultiply by the inverse already found.

marking_criteria.description_html: Transpose and divide to obtain the inverse.

questions.title: Recovering an inverse from a scaled identity
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & p & 2\\0 & 2 & 1\\1 & 0 & q\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}8 & -12 & -1\\1 & 2 & -1\\-2 & 3 & 2\end{pmatrix}\). It is known that \(AB=cI_3\) for a real number \(c\).

  1. Find \(p,q,c\).

    [4]

  2. Deduce \(A^{-1}\) and find \(\det B\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[p=3,\qquad q=4,\qquad c=7\]

(b)

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{8}{7} & - \dfrac{12}{7} & - \dfrac{1}{7}\\\dfrac{1}{7} & \dfrac{2}{7} & - \dfrac{1}{7}\\- \dfrac{2}{7} & \dfrac{3}{7} & \dfrac{2}{7}\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det B=49\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}p + 4 & 2 p - 6 & 3 - p\\0 & 7 & 0\\8 - 2 q & 3 q - 12 & 2 q - 1\end{pmatrix}\]

Entry (1,2) must be zero, giving \(2p-6=0\) and \(p=3\). Entry (3,1) gives \(8-2q=0\), so \(q=4\). Every diagonal entry is then 7, hence \(c=7\). All other off-diagonal entries also vanish.

(b)

Since \(AB=7I\), \(A(B/7)=I\). Therefore \(A^{-1}=B/7\). Also \(\det A=7\), so \(7\det B=\det(7I_3)=7^3\), giving \(\det B=49\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use off-diagonal entries first, since c does not appear in them.

(b)

The determinant of 7I₃ is 7³, not 7.

marking_criteria.description_html: Divide the known factor by 7 to obtain the inverse.
Find det B=49 with the correct dimension factor.

questions.title: The inverse of a three-by-three product
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\2 & 1 & 0\\-1 & 3 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & 0\\0 & 1 & 2\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find \(A^{-1}\) and \(B^{-1}\).

    [5]

  2. Hence find \((AB)^{-1}\).

    [3]

  3. State \(\det((AB)^{-1})\) without expanding another determinant.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The determinants are 1 and 2 respectively. The cofactor matrices are

\[C_A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -2 & 7\\0 & 1 & -3\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[C_B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\-1 & 2 & 0\\2 & -4 & 2\end{pmatrix}\]

Transpose each cofactor matrix and divide by its determinant:

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\-2 & 1 & 0\\7 & -3 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[B^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{2} & - \dfrac{1}{2} & 1\\0 & 1 & -2\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

The (3,1) entry of \(A^{-1}\) accounts for the interaction between the two sub-diagonal entries; it is not obtained by merely changing a sign.

(b)

\[(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{2} & - \dfrac{1}{2} & 1\\0 & 1 & -2\\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\-2 & 1 & 0\\7 & -3 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{17}{2} & - \dfrac{7}{2} & 1\\-16 & 7 & -2\\7 & -3 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\det((AB)^{-1})=\frac1{\det A\det B}=\frac12\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Exploit triangular structure but verify every off-diagonal entry.

(b)

The inverse of B comes first in the product.

(c)

Use the product and inverse determinant rules.

questions.title: When the inverse is symmetric
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}k + 1 & 2 k\\1 & k\end{pmatrix}\). A matrix is called symmetric when it equals its transpose.

  1. Find \(A^{-1}\) and state its restrictions.

    [3]

  2. Find the value of \(k\) for which \(A^{-1}\) is symmetric, and give that inverse.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det A=k(k+1)-2k=k(k-1)\]
\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{k - 1} & - \dfrac{2}{k - 1}\\- \dfrac{1}{k^{2} - k} & \dfrac{k + 1}{k^{2} - k}\end{pmatrix}\]

The two zero-determinant values must be excluded.

(b)

For a 2×2 matrix, symmetry requires its two off-diagonal entries to agree. Since the determinant is non-zero,

\[-2k=-1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k=\frac12\]

This is an allowed value. Substituting gives

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-2 & 4\\4 & -6\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

First find k(k−1).

(b)

Equate only the off-diagonal entries, without forgetting the restrictions.

questions.title: Updating a matrix solution efficiently
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 2\\0 & 1 & -1\\1 & 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(C=\begin{pmatrix}7 & -2\\-4 & 2\\2 & 0\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find \(A^{-1}\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(X\) such that \(AX=C\).

    [2]

  3. The entries in the first row of \(C\) are both increased by 1, forming \(C_1\). Without recomputing the entire product, find \(Y\) such that \(AY=C_1\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det A=1\]
\[C_A=\begin{pmatrix}3 & -1 & -1\\4 & -1 & -2\\-2 & 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

Transpose the cofactor matrix to obtain

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 4 & -2\\-1 & -1 & 1\\-1 & -2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[X=A^{-1}C=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\-1 & 0\\3 & -2\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Subtract the two equations: \(A(Y-X)=C_1-C\). Thus

\[Y-X=A^{-1}(C_1-C)=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 3\\-1 & -1\\-1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]

Each column of the change is the first column of \(A^{-1}\). Add this to X to get

\[Y=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 5\\-2 & -1\\2 & -3\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The determinant is 1, but the transpose of the cofactor matrix is still essential.

(b)

Premultiply by A⁻¹.

(c)

The change in each output column is (1,0,0)ᵀ.

marking_criteria.description_html: Express the update as A⁻¹ times the change.
Give the update using the first column of A⁻¹.

questions.title: Three factors and a scalar multiplier
questions.prompt_html:
The matrices \(A,B,C\) are non-singular 3×3 matrices. Their determinants are 2, −3 and 5 respectively.

  1. Prove, by showing the required cancellations, that \((ABC)^{-1}=C^{-1}B^{-1}A^{-1}\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(\det((2ABC)^{-1})\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[A B(CC^{-1})B^{-1}A^{-1}=A(BB^{-1})A^{-1}=I\]
\[C^{-1}B^{-1}(A^{-1}A)BC=C^{-1}(B^{-1}B)C=I\]

Both products are I, so the claimed matrix is the inverse.

(b)

\[\det(ABC)=2(-3)(5)=-30\]
\[\det(2ABC)=2^3(-30)=-240\]

The determinant of the inverse is the reciprocal, hence \(-1/240\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Regroup adjacent inverse pairs without interchanging factors.

(b)

Multiplying a 3×3 matrix by 2 multiplies its determinant by 8.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use associativity to cancel the forward product.

questions.title: The inverse of a sum of inverses
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Verify algebraically that \(A^{-1}+B^{-1}=B^{-1}(A+B)A^{-1}\). Hence express \((A^{-1}+B^{-1})^{-1}\) using \(A,B\) and \((A+B)^{-1}\).

    [4]

  2. Find \((A^{-1}+B^{-1})^{-1}\) numerically.

    [3]

  3. State the area multiplier of the plane transformation represented by this matrix.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[B^{-1}(A+B)A^{-1}=B^{-1}AA^{-1}+B^{-1}BA^{-1}=B^{-1}+A^{-1}\]

Here \(\det(A+B)=8\ne0\), so every factor is invertible. Reverse the order on taking the inverse:

\[(B^{-1}(A+B)A^{-1})^{-1}=A(A+B)^{-1}B\]

(b)

\[A+B=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[(A+B)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{3}{8} & - \dfrac{1}{8}\\- \dfrac{1}{8} & \dfrac{3}{8}\end{pmatrix}\]
\[A(A+B)^{-1}B=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{3}{4} & \dfrac{1}{4}\\\dfrac{1}{4} & \dfrac{3}{4}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\left|\frac{\det A\det B}{\det(A+B)}\right|=\frac{2\cdot2}{8}=\frac12\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the supplied factorisation without commuting any factors.

(b)

Use the factorisation from part (a).

(c)

Use the determinant of the product expression.

marking_criteria.description_html: Invert the three factors in reverse order.

questions.title: A determinant with one exceptional parameter
questions.prompt_html:
The matrix \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & 1\\0 & 1 & 3\\2 & 5 & t\end{pmatrix}\) depends on the real number \(t\).

  1. Find the value of \(t\) for which \(A\) is singular.

    [3]

  2. For that value of \(t\), find \(u,v\) such that \(A\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) is the zero column. Explain why this rules out an inverse.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det A=(t-15)-2(-6)-2=t-5\]

Thus the only singular value is \(t=5\).

(b)

The second component is \(v-3\), so \(v=3\). The first is \(u+2v-1\), giving \(u=-5\). The last component is then \(-10+15-5=0\).

If an inverse existed, multiplying \(A(-5,3,-1)^{\mathsf T}=0\) by it would imply the non-zero column \((-5,3,-1)^{\mathsf T}\) was zero, a contradiction.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand along the first row.

(b)

Use the second component first; all three must vanish.

marking_criteria.description_html: Equate components of the product to zero.
Assume an inverse and premultiply the zero-product equation.
Identify the contradiction with a non-zero column.

questions.title: Three singular values
questions.prompt_html:
For real \(t\), let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}t & 1 & 0\\1 & t & 1\\0 & 1 & t\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find every value of \(t\) for which \(A\) is singular.

    [3]

  2. When \(t=\sqrt2\), find a non-zero column \(v\) with first entry 1 such that \(Av=0\). Explain why \(A^{-1}\) cannot be used to solve this equation.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det A=t(t^2-1)-t=t(t^2-2)\]

Setting this equal to zero gives \(t=0,\sqrt2,-\sqrt2\).

(b)

Write \(v=(1,u,w)^{\mathsf T}\). The first row gives \(u=-\sqrt2\); the third gives \(w=1\). The middle row gives \(1-2+1=0\), so all three components vanish.

The determinant is zero, so \(A^{-1}\) does not exist. Multiplying by a supposed inverse would also contradict \(v\ne0\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Factor the determinant completely.

(b)

Use the first and third components and verify the middle one.

marking_criteria.description_html: Connect the zero determinant to the lack of an inverse.
Explain why the inverse method is invalid here.

questions.title: Inverse restrictions and two admissible values
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}t & 1 & 2\\2 & t + 1 & 0\\0 & 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}\), where \(t\) is real.

  1. Find all values of \(t\) for which \(A^{-1}\) exists.

    [3]

  2. For such \(t\), find \(A^{-1}\).

    [3]

  3. Find all real \(t\) for which \(\det(A^{-1})=1/12\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[t\in\mathbb R\setminus\{-2,1\}\]

(b)

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{t + 1}{t^{2} + t - 2} & - \dfrac{1}{t^{2} + t - 2} & \dfrac{- 2 t - 2}{3 t^{2} + 3 t - 6}\\- \dfrac{2}{t^{2} + t - 2} & \dfrac{t}{t^{2} + t - 2} & \dfrac{4}{3 t^{2} + 3 t - 6}\\0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[t=2\quad\text{or}\quad t=-3\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det A=3\{t(t+1)-2\}=3(t+2)(t-1)\]

The inverse exists exactly when this is non-zero.

(b)

The cofactors are

\[\begin{pmatrix}3 t + 3 & -6 & 0\\-3 & 3 t & 0\\- 2 t - 2 & 4 & t^{2} + t - 2\end{pmatrix}\]

Transpose and divide by \(3(t+2)(t-1)\).

\[A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{t + 1}{t^{2} + t - 2} & - \dfrac{1}{t^{2} + t - 2} & \dfrac{- 2 t - 2}{3 t^{2} + 3 t - 6}\\- \dfrac{2}{t^{2} + t - 2} & \dfrac{t}{t^{2} + t - 2} & \dfrac{4}{3 t^{2} + 3 t - 6}\\0 & 0 & \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

Computing the determinant of the inverse in part (b) gives \(1/[3(t+2)(t-1)]\). Hence

\[3(t+2)(t-1)=12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(t-2)(t+3)=0\]

Thus t=2 or t=−3; both solutions avoid \(-2,1\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand along the last row.

(b)

Keep the determinant factorised while simplifying.

(c)

Check both roots against the excluded values.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use cofactors or a valid inverse calculation.

questions.title: Signed determinants, unsigned areas
questions.prompt_html:
The matrix \(M=\begin{pmatrix}t + 1 & t - 2\\2 t + 1 & 2 t - 1\end{pmatrix}\) maps a triangle of area 4 onto a triangle of area 12.

  1. Find \(\det M\) in terms of \(t\).

    [2]

  2. Find all possible real values of \(t\).

    [3]

  3. For the negative value of \(t\), find \(M^{-1}\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\det M=4t+1\]

(b)

\[t=\frac12\quad\text{or}\quad t=-1\]

(c)

\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\- \dfrac{1}{3} & 0\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det M=(t+1)(2t-1)-(t-2)(2t+1)=4t+1\]

(b)

\[4|4t+1|=12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad4t+1=3\ \text{or}\ 4t+1=-3\]

The resulting values are \(1/2\) and \(-1\). Both are non-singular.

(c)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -3\\-1 & -3\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det M=-3\]
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\- \dfrac{1}{3} & 0\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand both products before subtracting.

(b)

Area uses the absolute determinant, so there are two sign cases.

(c)

Substitute the chosen parameter before inverting.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the inverse formula on the correct numerical matrix.

questions.title: A repeated factor in a determinant
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}t & 1 & 1\\1 & t & 1\\1 & 1 & t\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Show that \(\det A=(t-1)^2(t+2)\).

    [3]

  2. State all singular values and find the range of \(t\) for which \(\det(A^{-1})>0\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\det A=(t-1)^2(t+2)\]

(b)

\[t=-2,1\text{ are singular};\qquad -2<t<1\ \text{or}\ t>1\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det A=t(t^2-1)-(t-1)+(1-t)=t^3-3t+2\]
\[t^3-3t+2=(t-1)(t^2+t-2)=(t-1)^2(t+2)\]

(b)

For other t, \(\det(A^{-1})=1/[(t-1)^2(t+2)]\). The squared factor is strictly positive when \(t\ne1\), so the sign is the sign of \(t+2\). Require \(t>-2\) and exclude \(t=1\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand along one row, then factor the cubic.

(b)

The repeated factor does not change sign, but its zero is still forbidden.

questions.title: A two-parameter matrix that is never singular
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & - a & b\\a & 1 & 0\\- b & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), where \(a,b\) are real.

  1. Prove that \(A\) is non-singular for all real \(a,b\).

    [3]

  2. Find the largest possible value of \(\det(A^{-1})\) and state when it occurs.

    [2]

  3. Given \(a=1\) and \(\det A=6\), find \(b\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det A=1-(-a)(a)+b(b)=1+a^2+b^2\]

Both squares are non-negative, so the determinant cannot vanish.

(b)

\[\det(A^{-1})=\frac1{1+a^2+b^2}\le1\]

Equality requires both squares to be zero, so \(a=b=0\).

(c)

\[1+1+b^2=6\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b^2=4\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand along the first row and look for a sum of squares.

(b)

Minimise the positive denominator.

(c)

Keep both real square roots.

questions.title: Using one entry of an inverse
questions.prompt_html:
The matrix \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & p & 0\\0 & 2 & 1\\3 & 0 & q\end{pmatrix}\) has determinant 12. The entry in row 1, column 1 of \(A^{-1}\) is \(\frac12\).

  1. Find \(p\) and \(q\) without calculating the complete inverse.

    [4]

  2. Find \(\det(3A^{-1})\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The (1,1) cofactor is \(2q\). The inverse entry therefore gives

\[\frac{2q}{12}=\frac12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q=3\]

Expanding the determinant of A gives \(2q+3p\). Hence \(6+3p=12\) and \(p=2\).

(b)

\[\det(3A^{-1})=3^3\det(A^{-1})=\frac{27}{12}=\frac94\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the cofactor formula for just the specified inverse entry.

(b)

There are three rows, so the scalar contributes 3³.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the correct scalar and inverse rules.

questions.title: Four transformations with the same area multiplier
questions.prompt_html:
A triangle of area 5 is transformed into a triangle of area 15 by \(M=\begin{pmatrix}k & 2\\3 & k\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find every real value of \(k\).

    [4]

  2. For each class of values, state \(\det(M^{-1})\) and the area multiplier of the inverse transformation.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[k=3,-3,\sqrt3,-\sqrt3\]

(b)

For \(k=\pm3\), the inverse determinant is \(1/3\). For \(k=\pm\sqrt3\), it is \(-1/3\). The inverse area multiplier is \(1/3\) in every case.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det M=k^2-6,\qquad 5|k^2-6|=15\]

If \(k^2-6=3\), then \(k=\pm3\). If \(k^2-6=-3\), then \(k=\pm\sqrt3\). All four give non-zero determinant.

(b)

The original determinant is 3 for \(k=\pm3\) and −3 for \(k=\pm\sqrt3\). Hence the inverse determinants are \(1/3\) and \(-1/3\), respectively. Their absolute values are both \(1/3\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Area does not determine the sign of the determinant.

(b)

Separate the signed determinant from the positive area multiplier.

marking_criteria.description_html: Calculate det M and use the area relation.

questions.title: Two square products of rectangular factors
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 & 0\\0 & 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0\\1 & 1\\0 & -1\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find \(AB\) and its determinant.

    [3]

  2. Find \(BA\) and show that it is singular.

    [3]

  3. Explain why these results do not contradict the rule \(\det(AB)=\det A\det B\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(AB)=-4\]

(b)

\[BA=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 2 & 0\\1 & 2 & 2\\0 & -1 & -2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(BA)=0\]

(c)

That rule requires square factors of the same order; A and B are rectangular.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(AB)=3(-1)-1(1)=-4\]

(b)

\[BA=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 2 & 0\\1 & 2 & 2\\0 & -1 & -2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(BA)=2\begin{vmatrix}2&2\\-1&-2\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\0&-2\end{vmatrix}=2(-2)-2(-2)=0\]

(c)

Neither det A nor det B is defined here. The two square products even have different orders, so the square-factor determinant theorem cannot be applied to these factors.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

AB has order 2×2.

(b)

BA has order 3×3, so evaluate that determinant separately.

(c)

Check the hypotheses of the determinant rule.

marking_criteria.description_html: State why the rule is not applicable.

questions.title: Row combinations as a matrix product
questions.prompt_html:
A non-singular 3×3 matrix A has rows \(u,v,w\) and determinant −2. A matrix B has rows \(3u,u+v,2v-w\), in that order.

  1. Find a numerical matrix \(K\) such that \(B=KA\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(\det B\) and \(\det(B^{-1}A)\).

    [4]

  3. A student proposes \(B^{-1}=K^{-1}A^{-1}\). State the correct expression.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Left multiplication takes combinations of the rows of A. The coefficients of u,v,w in the three new rows are \((3,0,0),(1,1,0),(0,2,-1)\). These form the rows of K.

\[K=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 0 & 0\\1 & 1 & 0\\0 & 2 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

K is triangular, with determinant \(3(1)(-1)=-3\). Thus \(\det B=(-3)(-2)=6\). Consequently,

\[\det(B^{-1}A)=\frac{\det A}{\det B}=-\frac26=-\frac13\]

(c)

Since \(B=KA\), the inverse reverses those two factors.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The row coefficients belong in the rows of a left multiplier.

(b)

Use the determinant product rule, including its signs.

(c)

Reverse the order of the actual product KA.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use a left multiplier to form row combinations.

questions.title: A shear, a rotation and fixed points
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(M=\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(2 \theta \right)} & - \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}\\\sin{\left(2 \theta \right)} & \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\k & 1\end{pmatrix}\), where \(0<\theta<\pi\) and \(k\ne0\).

  1. Describe both transformations represented in this product and state their order.

    [3]

  2. Express \(M^{-1}\) as a product of two non-identity matrices.

    [2]

  3. Find the condition relating \(k\) and \(\tan\theta\) for \(M-I\) to be singular. Justify any division used.

    [5]

  4. Take \(k=-2\) and \(\theta=\pi/4\). Find all invariant points and show that they form a line.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

A shear with the y-axis fixed, \((1,0)\mapsto(1,k)\), followed by an anticlockwise rotation through \(2\theta\) about the origin.

(b)

\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\- k & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(2 \theta \right)} & \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}\\- \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)} & \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[\tan\theta=-\frac{k}{2}\]

(d)

\[y=x\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The right-hand matrix acts first. Its coordinate rule is \((x,y)\mapsto(x,kx+y)\), which fixes every point on the y-axis. The left-hand matrix is the standard rotation matrix.

(b)

Undo the rotation first, then the shear. Inverse factors appear in reverse order:

\[(RS)^{-1}=S^{-1}R^{-1}\]
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\- k & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(2 \theta \right)} & \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}\\- \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)} & \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}- k \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)} + \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)} & - \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}\\k \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)} + \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)} & \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(M-I)=2-2\cos2\theta+k\sin2\theta=0\]
\[4\sin^2\theta+2k\sin\theta\cos\theta=0\]

Here \(\sin\theta>0\). If \(\cos\theta=0\), the left side is 4, not zero. Division by \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta\) is therefore valid and gives \(2\tan\theta+k=0\).

(d)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1\\1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M\binom{x}{y}=\binom{2x-y}{x}=\binom{x}{y}\]

Both equations reduce to \(y=x\). Conversely every point \((x,x)\) is unchanged, so this is the complete fixed-point line.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

For column vectors the right-hand factor acts first.

(b)

Reverse the order and invert each factor.

(c)

Expand det(M−I), then use double-angle identities.

(d)

Invariant points satisfy Mv=v, not just Y=mX.

marking_criteria.description_html: Identify a shear fixing the y-axis with the correct example image.
Identify the rotation angle, direction and centre.
Give the entire line y=x and verify the converse.

questions.title: Exactly one invariant line after a rotation
questions.prompt_html:
A rotation anticlockwise through \(\theta\) about the origin is followed by a stretch parallel to the x-axis with factor \(3+2\sqrt2\). Let \(0\le\theta\le\pi\).

  1. Write the matrix \(M\) representing the combined transformation.

    [2]

  2. Find all values of \(\theta\) for which there is exactly one invariant line through the origin. Give that line for each angle.

    [9]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The rotation is first, so its matrix is on the right of the stretch matrix.

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}2 \sqrt{2} + 3 & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\\sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\left(2 \sqrt{2} + 3\right) \cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \left(2 \sqrt{2} + 3\right) \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\\sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Write \(h=3+2\sqrt2\). For \(y=mx\), the image coordinates satisfy \(Y=mX\) exactly when

\[h\sin\theta\,m^2-(h-1)\cos\theta\,m+\sin\theta=0\]

For \(0<\theta<\pi\), the vertical line is not invariant because its image has x-coordinate \(-h\sin\theta\,y\). The slope equation has exactly one real root when

\[\Delta=(h-1)^2\cos^2\theta-4h\sin^2\theta=4h(2\cos^2\theta-1)=0\]

Thus \(\theta=\pi/4,3\pi/4\). The repeated slope is \((h-1)\cos\theta/(2h\sin\theta)\), equal to \(\sqrt2-1\) and \(-(\sqrt2-1)\) respectively. At \(\theta=0,\pi\) both coordinate axes are invariant, so the endpoints are excluded.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use stretch × rotation, not rotation × stretch.

(b)

Use the slope discriminant, but check the vertical line and both endpoint angles separately.

marking_criteria.description_html: Place the factors in the correct order.
Exclude θ=0 and π because each has two invariant axes.
Give the correct invariant line at each angle.

questions.title: Recovering a stretch and a shear
questions.prompt_html:
A stretch parallel to the y-axis with positive factor \(a\) is followed by a shear fixing the y-axis and sending \((1,0)\) to \((1,b)\), where \(b>0\). Their combined matrix is \(M\).

  1. Find \(M\).

    [2]

  2. Find the matrix which maps the image of the unit square back onto the original square, with corresponding vertices restored.

    [2]

  3. The image of the unit square has area 4. The line \(y=-2x\) is invariant. Find \(a\) and \(b\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\b & a\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\- \dfrac{b}{a} & \dfrac{1}{a}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[a=4,\qquad b=6\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\b & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & a\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\b & a\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Restoring corresponding points requires the inverse, not merely a matrix giving the same area.

\[\det M=a\]
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\- \dfrac{b}{a} & \dfrac{1}{a}\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

The area scale factor is \(|\det M|=a\), so \(a=4\). A point \((x,-2x)\) maps to \((x,(b-2a)x)\). To stay on the same line, \(b-2a=-2\), hence \(b=6\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Apply the stretch first.

(b)

Use the inverse matrix.

(c)

Use the determinant for area and substitute a general point from the line.

marking_criteria.description_html: Transform a general point on the specified line.

questions.title: A singular transformation with changing fixed points
questions.prompt_html:
The transformation \(T_k\) has matrix \(M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\k & 2 k\end{pmatrix}\), where \(k\in\mathbb R\).

  1. Show that \(M\) is singular for every \(k\) and find the equation of the line containing all image points.

    [4]

  2. Find all invariant points, treating \(k=0\) and \(k\ne0\) separately.

    [3]

  3. Find all real \(k\) for which \(M^2=M\). Explain geometrically what happens on applying \(T_k\) twice in that case.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\det M=0,\qquad Y=kX\]

(b)

For \(k=0\): every point on \(y=0\). For \(k\ne0\): only \((0,0)\).

(c)

\[k=0\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det M=2k-2k=0\]
\[X=x+2y,\qquad Y=k(x+2y)=kX\]

Every point on \(Y=kX\) occurs: choose \((x,y)=(X,0)\).

(b)

The fixed-point equations are \(x+2y=x\) and \(k(x+2y)=y\). The first gives \(y=0\) and the second becomes \(kx=0\). If k=0, the whole x-axis is fixed; if k is non-zero, only the origin is fixed.

(c)

\[M^2=(1+2k)M\]

As \(M\ne0\), equality with \(M\) requires \(k=0\). For this value the first application places every point on the x-axis, and every point on that axis is fixed, so the second application changes nothing.

(a)

Factor the second image coordinate.

(b)

Solve Mv=v, not Mv=0.

(c)

Calculate M² directly.

questions.title: Two shears and preserved area
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\\dfrac{1}{4} & 1\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Describe the transformations represented by \(A\) and \(B\) fully.

    [4]

  2. Show that a triangle and its image under \(AB\) have equal areas.

    [2]

  3. Find all invariant lines through the origin under \(AB\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

A: shear fixing the x-axis, \((0,1)\mapsto(2,1)\). B: shear fixing the y-axis, \((1,0)\mapsto(1,1/4)\).

(b)

\[\det(AB)=1\]

(c)

\[y=\frac14x,\qquad y=-\frac12x\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The coordinate rules are \(A:(x,y)\mapsto(x+2y,y)\) and \(B:(x,y)\mapsto(x,x/4+y)\). These identify the fixed axes and shear amounts.

(b)

\[AB=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{3}{2} & 2\\\dfrac{1}{4} & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det(AB)=\frac32-\frac12=1\]

The area multiplier is the absolute determinant, hence 1.

(c)

\[X=\frac32x+2y,\qquad Y=\frac14x+y\]

For \(y=mx\), impose \(Y=mX\):

\[\frac14+m=m\left(\frac32+2m\right)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 8m^2+2m-1=(4m-1)(2m+1)=0\]

Thus \(m=1/4,-1/2\). The vertical line is not invariant because \((0,y)\mapsto(2y,y)\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use a point on each fixed axis and one point off it.

(b)

Multiply AB or evaluate its determinant directly.

(c)

Check x=0 separately from y=mx.

questions.title: A plane map that vanishes after two steps
questions.prompt_html:
The plane transformation \(T\) is represented by \(M=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1\\4 & -2\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find the line containing all image points and find all points mapped to \((3,6)\).

    [4]

  2. Find all invariant points.

    [2]

  3. Calculate \(M^2\) and explain the result in terms of the image line from part (a).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[Y=2X;\qquad (x,y)=(t,2t-3),\quad t\in\mathbb R\]

(b)

Only \((0,0)\).

(c)

\[M^2=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[X=2x-y,\qquad Y=4x-2y=2X\]

Every value of X is possible, so the full image is \(Y=2X\). For image \((3,6)\), the condition is \(2x-y=3\), giving the stated family.

(b)

The equations \(2x-y=x\) and \(4x-2y=y\) give \(y=x\) and then \(4x=3x\). Thus \(x=y=0\).

(c)

\[M^2=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

The first image lies on \(Y=2X\). Applying M to any point \((X,2X)\) produces \((0,0)\). Therefore two applications send the entire plane to the origin.

(a)

The two image equations are dependent.

(b)

Fixed points must satisfy both Mv=v equations.

(c)

Apply the map to a general point on its image line.

questions.title: Images of lines and invariant directions
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(M=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 3\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find \(M^{-1}\) and explain why every image point has exactly one preimage.

    [3]

  2. Find the equation of the image of the line \(y=x+1\). Use \((X,Y)\) for image coordinates.

    [3]

  3. Find all invariant lines through the origin.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\det M=4-3=1\]
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -3\\-1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\]

For each image column w, the unique preimage is \(M^{-1}w\). If two preimages had the same image, premultiplying by the inverse would make them equal.

(b)

Substitute \(x=2X-3Y\) and \(y=-X+2Y\) from the inverse into \(y=x+1\).

\[-X+2Y=2X-3Y+1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad5Y-3X=1\]

(c)

\[1+2m=m(2+3m)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad3m^2=1\]

The lines are \(y=x/\sqrt3\) and \(y=-x/\sqrt3\). The vertical line is not invariant, because \((0,y)\mapsto(3y,2y)\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

A non-zero determinant gives a reversible map.

(b)

Substitute inverse coordinates into the original line.

(c)

Use Y=mX and then check x=0.

questions.title: Deriving a reflection in an oblique line
questions.prompt_html:
A reflection in \(y=2x\) is represented by \(M\).

  1. Explain why \(M\binom12=\binom12\) and \(M\binom{-2}{1}=\binom2{-1}\). Hence find \(M\).

    [5]

  2. Find the image of \((5,0)\) and verify that applying the reflection a second time returns this point.

    [2]

  3. State the area multiplier.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The first vector lies on the mirror line and is fixed. The second is perpendicular to it, since \(1(-2)+2(1)=0\), and reflection reverses that vector. Thus

\[M\begin{pmatrix}1 & -2\\2 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\2 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\2 & -1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{5} & \dfrac{2}{5}\\- \dfrac{2}{5} & \dfrac{1}{5}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{3}{5} & \dfrac{4}{5}\\\dfrac{4}{5} & \dfrac{3}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[M\begin{pmatrix}5\\0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M\begin{pmatrix}-3\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

The determinant is −1, so its absolute value is 1.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use one direction along the mirror and one perpendicular to it.

(b)

Multiply the image column by the same matrix.

(c)

Reflections preserve area.

marking_criteria.description_html: Form a matrix equation from the two images.

questions.title: The order of two shears
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(S=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(T=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\-1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Describe fully the shear represented by each matrix.

    [2]

  2. Find \(ST\) and \(TS\). Give the two different images of \((1,1)\) under these composites.

    [3]

  3. Show that applying either composite twice has the same geometrical effect. Describe this effect fully.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

S fixes the x-axis and sends \((0,1)\) to \((2,1)\). T fixes the y-axis and sends \((1,0)\) to \((1,-1)\).

(b)

\[ST=\begin{pmatrix}-1 & 2\\-1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[TS=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\-1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]

The images are \((1,0)\) and \((3,-2)\), respectively.

(c)

\[(ST)^2=(TS)^2=-I_2\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The coordinate rules are \(S:(x,y)\mapsto(x+2y,y)\) and \(T:(x,y)\mapsto(x,y-x)\). These identify the fixed axes and shear directions.

(b)

\[ST=\begin{pmatrix}-1 & 2\\-1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[TS=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\-1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[ST\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
\[TS\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

(c)

\[(ST)^2=\begin{pmatrix}-1 & 0\\0 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[(TS)^2=\begin{pmatrix}-1 & 0\\0 & -1\end{pmatrix}\]

The matrix −I₂ sends \((x,y)\) to \((-x,-y)\). It is a rotation through \(\pi\) about the origin.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Read the image coordinates from each product with (x,y)ᵀ.

(b)

The rightmost shear acts first.

(c)

Square each product, then recognise the coordinate rule.
