Describe T with fixed axis and example image.

questions.title: Recognising a composite as a single reflection
questions.prompt_html:
A reflection in the x-axis is followed by an anticlockwise rotation through \(\pi/3\) about the origin.

  1. Find the matrix \(M\) of the composite transformation.

    [3]

  2. Find the line of invariant points.

    [2]

  3. Show that the composite is a reflection in this line, not merely a transformation fixing the line.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{2} & \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & - \dfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[y=\frac{x}{\sqrt3}\]

(c)

It fixes the direction \((\sqrt3,1)\) and reverses the perpendicular direction \((-1,\sqrt3)\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{2} & - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\0 & -1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{2} & \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & - \dfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Solve \(M\binom xy=\binom xy\). The first component gives

\[\frac12x+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}y=x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\sqrt3 y\]

The second component gives the same condition.

(c)

\[M\begin{pmatrix}-1\\\sqrt{3}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\- \sqrt{3}\end{pmatrix}\]

This is the negative of the input vector. Every point can be resolved into components along these two perpendicular directions. M leaves the parallel component unchanged and reverses the perpendicular component: exactly reflection in \(y=x/\sqrt3\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Apply the reflection first, so its matrix is on the right.

(b)

Invariant points satisfy Mv=v, not just that the image is parallel to v.

(c)

Check what happens to a perpendicular direction as well.

marking_criteria.description_html: Set the image equal to the original point.
Explain why the two component rules identify the reflection.

questions.title: Undoing a stretch, rotation and shear
questions.prompt_html:
A transformation first stretches parallel to the x-axis with factor 2, then rotates anticlockwise through \(\pi/2\) about the origin, and finally applies a shear fixing the y-axis and mapping \((1,0)\) to \((1,3)\).

  1. Find the matrix \(M\) of the transformation.

    [3]

  2. Find \(M^{-1}\) and describe the operations of the inverse transformation in order.

    [3]

  3. Find the preimage of \((4,-2)\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\2 & -3\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{3}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2}\\-1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

Shear fixing the y-axis with \((1,0)\mapsto(1,-3)\); clockwise rotation through \(\pi/2\) about the origin; stretch parallel to the x-axis with factor \(1/2\).

(c)

\[\binom xy=\begin{pmatrix}-7\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\3 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\2 & -3\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{2} & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\-1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\-3 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{3}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2}\\-1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

The rightmost factor undoes the last shear first. Then undo the rotation and finally the stretch.

(c)

\[\binom xy=M^{-1}\binom4{-2}=\begin{pmatrix}-7\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Write the matrices in reverse chronological order.

(b)

Reverse both the factors and the physical operations.

(c)

Use the inverse, not the forward map.

marking_criteria.description_html: Apply the inverse to the given output.

questions.title: Images and preimages of lines
questions.prompt_html:
The matrix \(M=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\3 & 4\end{pmatrix}\) maps \((x,y)\) to \((X,Y)\).

  1. Find the equation of the image of the line \(x=2\).

    [3]

  2. Find the equation of the line whose image is \(2X-Y=5\).

    [2]

  3. Find the input point whose image is the intersection of \(Y-2X=2\) and \(X+Y=8\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The coordinate rule is \(X=x+2y\), \(Y=3x+4y\). Eliminating y gives \(Y-2X=x\). Thus the image of \(x=2\) is \(Y-2X=2\). Since M is non-singular, this is the whole image line.

(b)

\[2(x+2y)-(3x+4y)=5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=-5\]

(c)

The output intersection is \((X,Y)=(2,6)\). Multiplication by \(M^{-1}\) gives

\[\binom xy=\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Eliminate y from the two output coordinates.

(b)

For a preimage, substitute the forward rule into the output equation.

(c)

Find the output intersection before applying the inverse.

questions.title: A family of invariant lines
questions.prompt_html:
The matrix \(M=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) acts on the plane.

  1. Find all invariant points.

    [2]

  2. Find all invariant straight lines, including those not passing through the origin.

    [4]

  3. Explain why \(y=2\) is invariant but is not a line of invariant points.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[x=0\]

(b)

\[y=c\ (c\in\mathbb R),\qquad x=0\]

(c)

Its points stay on the same line, but only (0,2) is fixed.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The rule is \((X,Y)=(3x,y)\). Equality with \((x,y)\) requires \(3x=x\), so \(x=0\), with y arbitrary.

(b)

For a non-vertical line \(y=mx+c\), use \(x=X/3\) and \(y=Y\) to obtain \(Y=(m/3)X+c\). Equality with the original line requires \(m/3=m\), hence \(m=0\), with any c. A vertical line \(x=d\) maps to \(X=3d\), so is invariant only when \(d=0\).

(c)

A point \((x,2)\) maps to \((3x,2)\), which is on \(y=2\). For \(x\ne0\), the position changes.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

A fixed point must have unchanged coordinates.

(b)

Consider non-vertical and vertical lines separately.

(c)

Distinguish setwise preservation from pointwise preservation.

marking_criteria.description_html: Set image coordinates equal to input coordinates.
Explain the distinction with the actual coordinate rule.

questions.title: Invariant lines of a reflection
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(M=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\-1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Describe the transformation fully and find its invariant points.

    [3]

  2. Find all invariant straight lines.

    [4]

  3. State the only fixed point on \(y=x+6\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

Reflection in \(y=-x\); the invariant points are exactly those on this line.

(b)

\[y=-x,\qquad y=x+c\quad(c\in\mathbb R)\]

(c)

\[(-3,3)\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The rule is \((X,Y)=(-y,-x)\). It fixes \((x,-x)\) and reverses the perpendicular direction \((1,1)\), so it is reflection in \(y=-x\). Setting the image equal to the input gives the same line.

(b)

For a point on \(y=mx+c\), require \(Y=mX+c\). Substitution gives

\[-x=-m(mx+c)+c=-m^2x+c(1-m)\]

Therefore \(m^2=1\) and \(c(1-m)=0\). If \(m=1\), any c works. If \(m=-1\), then \(c=0\). A vertical line \(x=d\) maps to the horizontal line \(Y=-d\), so no vertical line is invariant.

(c)

Intersect \(y=x+6\) with the fixed-point line \(y=-x\). This gives \(2x=-6\) and the point \((-3,3)\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Check the line y=−x and the perpendicular direction.

(b)

A reflected line may remain the same set without being fixed point by point.

(c)

A fixed point must also lie on the mirror line.

marking_criteria.description_html: Identify the reflection and its mirror line.
Give the full set of fixed points.

questions.title: A parameter controls the number of invariant directions
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(M=\begin{pmatrix}t & 1\\-2 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), where \(t\ne-2\).

  1. Explain the restriction \(t\ne-2\). Derive an equation for the gradient \(m\) of an invariant line through the origin.

    [4]

  2. Classify the permitted values of \(t\) giving no invariant line, exactly one invariant line, or two invariant lines through the origin.

    [4]

  3. Find all invariant points for any permitted \(t\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\det M=t+2,\qquad m^2+(t-1)m+2=0\]

(b)

None: \(1-2\sqrt2<t<1+2\sqrt2\). Exactly one: \(t=1\pm2\sqrt2\). Two: \(t<1-2\sqrt2\) or \(t>1+2\sqrt2\), with \(t=-2\) excluded.

(c)

Only the origin.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The determinant is \(t+2\), so the restriction ensures a non-singular transformation. On \(y=mx\), the image is \(((t+m)x,(m-2)x)\). Requiring \(Y=mX\) gives \(m-2=m(t+m)\), and hence the equation. The vertical line is not invariant since \((0,y)\mapsto(y,y)\).

(b)

\[\Delta=(t-1)^2-8\]

The quadratic in m has zero, one or two real roots according as this discriminant is negative, zero or positive. Keep the original exclusion of \(t=-2\) in the positive-discriminant case.

(c)

Since \(\det(M-I)=2\ne0\), the equation \((M-I)v=0\) has only \(v=0\): multiply by the inverse of M−I.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Treat the vertical line separately from y=mx.

(b)

Use the discriminant of the gradient equation, not det M.

(c)

Fixed points satisfy (M−I)v=0.

marking_criteria.description_html: Justify that only the origin is fixed.

questions.title: The invariant line a gradient method can miss
questions.prompt_html:
The matrix \(M=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0\\3 & -1\end{pmatrix}\) represents a plane transformation.

  1. Find every invariant line through the origin.

    [4]

  2. Describe what happens to points on each of these lines and find all fixed points.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[x=0,\qquad y=x\]

(b)

On \(y=x\), points are enlarged by factor 2 from the origin. On \(x=0\), points are reversed through the origin. Only the origin is fixed.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For \(y=mx\), the image is \((2x,(3-m)x)\). Thus \(3-m=2m\), so \(m=1\). In addition, \((0,y)\mapsto(0,-y)\), so the vertical line \(x=0\) is invariant. These exhaust the possible directions.

(b)

\[M\binom xx=2\binom xx,\qquad M\binom0y=-\binom0y\]

Neither rule fixes a non-zero point. Alternatively, \(2x=x\) gives \(x=0\), then \(-y=y\) gives \(y=0\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Do not assume that every line has a finite gradient.

(b)

An invariant direction does not imply fixed points.

marking_criteria.description_html: State that only the origin is fixed.

questions.title: Two possible lines of fixed points
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(M=\begin{pmatrix}t & 2\\3 & t - 1\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find all values of \(t\) for which the transformation has a line of invariant points.

    [3]

  2. For each value, find the complete line of invariant points.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[t=-1\quad\text{or}\quad t=4\]

(b)

\[t=-1:\ y=x;\qquad t=4:\ 3x+2y=0\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

A non-zero fixed point solves \((M-I)v=0\), so M−I must be singular:

\[\det(M-I)=(t-1)(t-2)-6=(t-4)(t+1)=0\]

These two values will each produce a line, as verified next. Neither makes M singular: its determinants are −4 and 6 respectively.

(b)

For \(t=-1\), the equations are \(-2x+2y=0\) and \(3x-3y=0\), giving \(y=x\). For \(t=4\), both equations reduce to \(3x+2y=0\). In each case a genuine line of solutions exists, not the whole plane.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use det(M−I)=0, not det M=0.

(b)

Substitute each value before simplifying the two equations.

marking_criteria.description_html: Solve the fixed-point equations in each case.

questions.title: Prescribed images along two lines
questions.prompt_html:
A linear transformation sends \((1,1)\) to \((2,2)\) and \((1,-2)\) to \((-3,6)\).

  1. Find its matrix \(M\).

    [3]

  2. Without using a new matrix multiplication, find the image of \((2,-1)\).

    [2]

  3. The triangle has vertices \((0,0),(1,1),(1,-2)\). Find the area of its image, and state two invariant lines.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{5}{3}\\\dfrac{10}{3} & - \dfrac{4}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[(2,-1)\mapsto(-1,8)\]

(c)

\[\text{Image area}=9;\qquad y=x,\ y=-2x\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[M\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\1 & -2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -3\\2 & 6\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M=\begin{pmatrix}2 & -3\\2 & 6\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{2}{3} & \dfrac{1}{3}\\\dfrac{1}{3} & - \dfrac{1}{3}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{5}{3}\\\dfrac{10}{3} & - \dfrac{4}{3}\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

The input is \((1,1)+(1,-2)\). Linearity gives the image \((2,2)+(-3,6)=(-1,8)\).

(c)

The original area is \(\frac12|1(-2)-1(1)|=\frac32\). Since \(|\det M|=6\), the image area is \(9\). Each supplied direction remains on the same line, so \(y=x\) and \(y=-2x\) are invariant.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Build a matrix equation using the two input columns.

(b)

Add the two supplied input columns.

(c)

Use the determinant for area and the supplied images for directions.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the correct inverse and multiplication order.
Express the input as the sum of the supplied vectors.
Find the original area and area multiplier.

questions.title: Invariant lines and fixed points of a shear
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(S=\begin{pmatrix}1 & k\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), where \(k\ne0\).

  1. Find all invariant points.

    [2]

  2. Find all invariant straight lines and justify that there are no others.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The rule is \((X,Y)=(x+ky,y)\). Fixed points require \(ky=0\). Since \(k\ne0\), precisely the x-axis is fixed.

(b)

On \(y=mx+c\), the equation \(Y=mX+c\) gives

\[mx+c=m(x+k(mx+c))+c\]

Comparing coefficients gives \(km^2=0\), hence \(m=0\); the constant c is unrestricted. A vertical line \(x=d\) maps to \(X=d+kY\), not a vertical line. Thus precisely the horizontal lines are invariant.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the assumption k≠0.

(b)

Check both finite-gradient and vertical lines.

questions.title: Area-preserving stretches and a fixed line
questions.prompt_html:
A stretch parallel to the x-axis with factor 2 and a stretch parallel to the y-axis with factor \(1/2\) are followed by an anticlockwise rotation through \(\theta\) about the origin, where \(0<\theta<\pi\).

  1. Find the composite matrix \(M\) and show that it preserves area.

    [3]

  2. Find the value of \(\theta\) for which there is a line of invariant points.

    [3]

  3. For this angle, find the fixed-point line and show that it is the only invariant line through the origin.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}2 \cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \dfrac{\sin{\left(\theta \right)}}{2}\\2 \sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \dfrac{\cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{2}\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\det M=1\]

(b)

\[\theta=\arccos\frac45\]

(c)

\[y=2x\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\\sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2 & 0\\0 & \dfrac{1}{2}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2 \cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \dfrac{\sin{\left(\theta \right)}}{2}\\2 \sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \dfrac{\cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{2}\end{pmatrix}\]

Each rotation has determinant 1, and the two stretches have product determinant \(2(1/2)=1\). The absolute determinant is therefore 1.

(b)

\[\det(M-I)=2-\frac52\cos\theta\]

A non-zero fixed point requires this determinant to vanish, so \(\cos\theta=4/5\). On the given interval this gives the single angle stated, with \(\sin\theta=3/5\).

(c)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{8}{5} & - \dfrac{3}{10}\\\dfrac{6}{5} & \dfrac{2}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]

The fixed-point equations reduce to \(2x-y=0\). For an invariant line \(y=mx\), the condition \(Y=mX\) simplifies to \((m-2)^2=0\). The vertical line is not invariant because the (1,2) entry of M is non-zero. Thus there is exactly one invariant direction, and its line is fixed pointwise.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The rotation is applied last and appears on the left.

(b)

Fixed points require a singular M−I.

(c)

Find fixed points first, then separately check all invariant directions.

marking_criteria.description_html: Select the unique angle in the given interval.
Exclude the vertical line and conclude uniqueness.

questions.title: Two shears: classifying invariant lines
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(S=\begin{pmatrix}1 & a\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(T=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\b & 1\end{pmatrix}\), where \(a,b\ne0\). Put \(M=ST\).

  1. Describe the transformations in the correct order and find \(M\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(M^{-1}\) and the area multiplier of the transformation.

    [3]

  3. Classify the values of \(ab\) for which M has zero, one or two invariant lines through the origin.

    [5]

  4. When \(a=2,b=-2\), find the invariant line and determine whether its non-zero points are fixed.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}a b + 1 & a\\b & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

First the shear T fixing the y-axis, then the shear S fixing the x-axis.

(b)

\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & - a\\- b & a b + 1\end{pmatrix}\]

Area multiplier: 1.

(c)

Zero if \(-4<ab<0\); one if \(ab=-4\); two if \(ab<-4\) or \(ab>0\).

(d)

\[y=x;\qquad M\binom{x}{x}=-\binom{x}{x}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

T sends \((1,0)\) to \((1,b)\) and S sends \((0,1)\) to \((a,1)\). Since the right factor acts first, apply T then S.

\[ST=\begin{pmatrix}a b + 1 & a\\b & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[\det M=1+ab-ab=1\]
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1 & - a\\- b & a b + 1\end{pmatrix}\]

The area multiplier is \(|1|=1\).

(c)

For \(y=mx\), require \(b+m=m(1+ab+am)\). Thus

\[am^2+abm-b=0,\qquad\Delta=ab(ab+4)\]

Since \(a\ne0\), this is a genuine quadratic. Its discriminant is negative when ab lies strictly between −4 and 0, zero at ab=−4, and positive when ab is below −4 or above 0. The value \(ab=0\) is excluded by the question. The vertical line is not invariant because \((0,y)\mapsto(ay,y)\) and \(a\ne0\).

(d)

The slope equation is \(2(m-1)^2=0\), so the line is \(y=x\). On this line M sends each point to its negative, so only the origin is fixed.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The product ST applies T first.

(b)

Use det M before finding its inverse.

(c)

Classify the sign of the slope discriminant; do not add the excluded case ab=0.

(d)

An invariant line need not consist of invariant points.

marking_criteria.description_html: Deal with vertical lines and the excluded value ab=0.
Show non-zero points are reversed, not fixed.

questions.title: Reconstructing a three-stage transformation
questions.prompt_html:
A stretch parallel to the x-axis with factor \(a>0\) is followed by a shear fixing the x-axis and sending \((0,1)\) to \((b,1)\). Finally there is a reflection in \(y=x\). The combined matrix is \(M\).

  1. Find \(M\) in terms of \(a,b\).

    [3]

  2. The unit square has image area 6, and \((1,2)\) maps to \((2,10)\). Find \(a,b\).

    [3]

  3. Find \(M^{-1}\) and describe the three operations that undo the original transformation, in the order applied.

    [3]

  4. Find all invariant lines through the origin.

    [3]

  5. Find the equation of the line whose image is \(X+Y=8\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\a & b\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[a=6,\qquad b=2\]

(c)

\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{6}\\1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

(d)

\[y=(1+\sqrt7)x,\qquad y=(1-\sqrt7)x\]

(e)

\[6x+3y=8\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & b\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\a & b\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

Since \(\det M=-a\) and \(a>0\), the area gives \(a=6\). The second image coordinate gives \(a+2b=10\), hence \(b=2\).

(c)

\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}- \dfrac{1}{3} & \dfrac{1}{6}\\1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\]

First reflect in \(y=x\), then apply the shear fixing the x-axis with \((0,1)\mapsto(-2,1)\), then stretch parallel to the x-axis with factor \(1/6\). This reverses both the operations and their order.

(d)

On \(y=mx\), the image is \((mx,(6+2m)x)\). Thus \(m^2-2m-6=0\), giving \(m=1\pm\sqrt7\). The vertical line maps onto \(Y=2X\), so is not invariant.

(e)

Substitute \(X=y\) and \(Y=6x+2y\) into the desired image equation: \(y+6x+2y=8\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The reflection matrix is the leftmost factor.

(b)

Use a>0 after taking the absolute determinant.

(c)

Undo the last operation first.

(d)

Use Y=mX and remember the vertical line.

(e)

This is a preimage question: substitute the forward coordinate rule.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the determinant and area to find a=6.

questions.title: Area, invariant lines and the image of a square
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(M=\begin{pmatrix}p & q\\q & p\end{pmatrix}\), where \(p>q>0\). The point \((1,1)\) maps to \((5,5)\), and the image of the unit square has area 15.

  1. Find \(p,q\).

    [4]

  2. Find all invariant lines through the origin and all invariant points.

    [4]

  3. Show that the image of the unit square is a rhombus but not a rectangle.

    [3]

  4. Find the matrix which maps this image back to the unit square.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[p=4,\qquad q=1\]

(b)

\[y=x,\quad y=-x;\qquad\text{only }(0,0)\text{ is fixed}\]

(c)

Adjacent side vectors are (4,1) and (1,4); both have length √17, but their scalar product is 8.

(d)

\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{4}{15} & - \dfrac{1}{15}\\- \dfrac{1}{15} & \dfrac{4}{15}\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The given image gives \(p+q=5\). Since \(p>q>0\), the determinant \((p-q)(p+q)\) is positive. Hence

\[(p-q)5=15\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p-q=3\]

Solving with \(p+q=5\) gives \(p=4,q=1\).

(b)

For \(y=mx\), \(Y=mX\) gives \(1+4m=m(4+m)\), hence \(m^2=1\). The vertical line is not invariant, as \((0,y)\mapsto(y,4y)\). For fixed points,

\[3x+y=0,\qquad x+3y=0\]

Substitution gives \(x=y=0\).

(c)

The vertices are \((0,0),(4,1),(5,5),(1,4)\). The two adjacent side lengths are both \(\sqrt{17}\), so all four sides of this parallelogram are equal. Their scalar product is \(4(1)+1(4)=8\ne0\), so the sides are not perpendicular and it is not a rectangle.

(d)

\[M^{-1}=\frac1{15}\begin{pmatrix}4&-1\\-1&4\end{pmatrix}\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The inequalities allow you to remove the absolute value in the area equation.

(b)

Apply separate equations for invariant lines and invariant points.

(c)

Use the two columns as adjacent side vectors.

(d)

Use the inverse, retaining the determinant factor.

marking_criteria.description_html: Show the angle is not a right angle.

questions.title: An algebraic family of reflections
questions.prompt_html:
For a real number \(t\), define \(M=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1 - t^{2}}{t^{2} + 1} & \dfrac{2 t}{t^{2} + 1}\\\dfrac{2 t}{t^{2} + 1} & \dfrac{t^{2} - 1}{t^{2} + 1}\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. By direct multiplication, show that \(M^2=I\) and deduce \(M^{-1}\).

    [3]

  2. Show that \(M\) represents reflection in \(y=tx\), including the case \(t=0\).

    [4]

  3. The point \((1,0)\) maps to \((-5/13,12/13)\). Find \(t\).

    [3]

  4. For this value of \(t\), find the image of \((1,0)\) after 87 successive applications.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[M^2=I,\qquad M^{-1}=M\]

(b)

The direction (1,t) is fixed and the perpendicular direction (−t,1) is reversed.

(c)

\[t=\frac32\]

(d)

\[(-5/13,12/13)\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The diagonal numerators of M² are \((1-t^2)^2+4t^2=(1+t^2)^2\). Each off-diagonal numerator is \(2t(1-t^2)+2t(t^2-1)=0\). Division by \((1+t^2)^2\) therefore gives I. Since \(M M=I\), its inverse is itself.

(b)

\[M\binom1t=\binom1t,\qquad M\binom{-t}1=-\binom{-t}1\]

The directions are perpendicular because \(1(-t)+t(1)=0\) and are independent for every real t. Thus M fixes the component along \(y=tx\) and reverses the perpendicular component. This is the defining reflection rule. When \(t=0\), M is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), reflection in the x-axis.

(c)

\[\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}=-\frac5{13}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t^2=\frac94\]

The second coordinate \(2t/(1+t^2)=12/13>0\) forces \(t>0\). Therefore \(t=3/2\).

(d)

Since \(M^2=I\), \(M^{87}=(M^2)^{43}M=M\). Thus the image is the same as after one application.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Calculate diagonal and off-diagonal entries symbolically.

(b)

A proof that M²=I alone would not distinguish a reflection from other transformations.

(c)

The first coordinate determines |t|; the second fixes its sign.

(d)

Pair the applications using M²=I.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the first coordinate to find t².

questions.title: Fixed points, invariant lines and two-step returns
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(M=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\).

  1. Find the complete set of invariant points.

    [2]

  2. Find all invariant straight lines, including those not through the origin.

    [6]

  3. Determine whether there is any point which returns to its starting position after two applications of M but is not fixed after one application.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[y=-x\]

(b)

\[y=c\ (c\in\mathbb R),\qquad y=-x\]

(c)

No such point exists.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The image is \((2x+y,y)\). It equals the input precisely when \(x+y=0\).

(b)

For \(y=mx+c\), the image is \(((2+m)x+c,mx+c)\). It lies on the same line exactly when

\[mx+c=m((2+m)x+c)+c\]

Comparing coefficients of x and constants gives \(m(m+1)=0\) and \(mc=0\). Thus \(m=0\) permits any c; \(m=-1\) requires \(c=0\). A vertical line \(x=d\) maps to \(X=2d+Y\), not a vertical line. Hence the list is complete.

(c)

\[M^2=\begin{pmatrix}4 & 3\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

Returning after two applications requires \(4x+3y=x\), hence \(x+y=0\). Every such point is already fixed by part (a). Therefore a two-step return without a one-step return is impossible.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The second coordinate is already unchanged.

(b)

Compare both the gradient and the constant term; then test vertical lines.

(c)

Solve M²v=v and compare with the fixed-point set of M.

marking_criteria.description_html: Set the first coordinate equal to x.
Justify that there are no additional lines.
Conclude that no point has exactly a two-step return.

questions.title: One invariant direction does not imply a fixed line
questions.prompt_html:
A stretch parallel to the x-axis with factor \(a>1\) is followed by an anticlockwise rotation through \(\theta\) about the origin, where \(0\le\theta\le\pi\). The composite matrix is M.

  1. Find \(M\) and write its inverse as a product of two standard transformation matrices.

    [3]

  2. The image of the unit square has area 9. Find \(a\).

    [1]

  3. For this value of \(a\), find every \(\theta\) for which there is exactly one invariant line through the origin, and find that line in each case.

    [6]

  4. Take the acute angle from part (c). Find the image of \(y=3x+c\) and determine which of these lines are invariant.

    [2]

  5. For the same acute angle, find all invariant points and describe the action on its invariant line.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}a \cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\a \sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]
\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{a} & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(\theta \right)} & \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\- \sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

\[a=9\]

(c)

\[\theta=\arccos\frac35:\ y=3x\]
\[\theta=\pi-\arccos\frac35:\ y=-3x\]

(d)

\[Y=3X+3c;\qquad c=0\text{ only}\]

(e)

Only the origin is fixed. On \(y=3x\), points are enlarged from the origin by factor 3.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\\sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}a \cos{\left(\theta \right)} & - \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\a \sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]

Undo the rotation first, then the stretch. Hence

\[M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{1}{a} & 0\\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\left(\theta \right)} & \sin{\left(\theta \right)}\\- \sin{\left(\theta \right)} & \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\end{pmatrix}\]

(b)

A rotation preserves area and the stretch multiplies it by \(a>1\). Equivalently \(|\det M|=a=9\).

(c)

For \(0<\theta<\pi\), a line \(y=mx\) is invariant when

\[\sin\theta\,m^2-8\cos\theta\,m+9\sin\theta=0\]

Exactly one finite gradient requires discriminant zero:

\[64\cos^2\theta-36\sin^2\theta=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\cos\theta=\pm\frac35\]

In both cases \(\sin\theta=4/5\). The repeated gradient is \(m=4\cos\theta/\sin\theta\), giving 3 and −3. The vertical line is not invariant in the open interval because \(\sin\theta\ne0\). At \(\theta=0,\pi\) the two coordinate axes are invariant, so those endpoints do not qualify.

(d)

\[M=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{27}{5} & - \dfrac{4}{5}\\\dfrac{36}{5} & \dfrac{3}{5}\end{pmatrix}\]

Substitution of \(y=3x+c\) gives \(X=3x-4c/5\) and \(Y=9x+3c/5\). Hence \(Y-3X=3c\). The original line and its image agree only when \(3c=c\), so \(c=0\).

(e)

\[M\binom{x}{3x}=3\binom{x}{3x}\]

No non-zero point of that line is fixed. More generally, \(\det(M-I)=4\ne0\), so the fixed-point equation has only the zero solution.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The chronological order of the inverse transformations is reversed.

(b)

Use the determinant, not the side lengths after rotation.

(c)

Check the discriminant and the endpoint angles separately.

(d)

The invariant direction is not sufficient: compare the intercepts too.

(e)

Compare the scale on the invariant line with 1.

marking_criteria.description_html: Justify that only the origin is fixed.
